statements: The chief complaint is a 1-month history of right lower back and abdominal pain in a 60-year-old man.
The patient’s main concern appears to be pain.
The key diagnostic finding is the incidentally/imaging-detected small right renal mass.
Ultrasound showed a 0.9 × 0.8 cm round hypoechoic mass in the mid-to-lower right renal parenchyma.
Ultrasound showed no internal blood flow in the mass.
CT angiography showed a 1 cm nodular iso-dense lesion in the mid-right kidney abutting the capsule.
CT angiography showed continuous, obvious but inhomogeneous arterial-phase enhancement of the lesion.
CT angiography showed no prominent feeding vessels.
The lesion is a small solid enhancing renal cortical/subcapsular mass.
Renal function is preserved overall.
The creatinine level is 73.5 μmol/L.
The split GFR is 34.9 mL/min bilaterally.
Physical examination is unremarkable.
CA 19-9 is elevated.
CA 19-9 is nonspecific.
CA 19-9 does not by itself define the renal lesion.
Thyroid ultrasound shows bilateral TI-RADS 3 nodules.
TI-RADS 3 nodules are low-suspicion thyroid nodules.
The thyroid nodules do not establish metastatic thyroid cancer.
There is no reported hematuria.
There are no constitutional symptoms.
There are no abnormal physical findings.
There is no evidence of a large infiltrative renal mass.
There are no prominent feeding vessels on CTA.
The absence of prominent feeding vessels argues somewhat against a classic hypervascular lesion with obvious vascular supply.
Ultrasound showed no internal blood flow.
The lesion is very small.
Doppler may be insensitive for the lesion.
There is no mention of macroscopic fat.
The lack of macroscopic fat makes angiomyolipoma less likely.
There is no cystic description.
A simple cyst is unlikely.
Renal hemangioblastoma fits a small, well-circumscribed renal parenchymal/subcapsular lesion with marked arterial enhancement.
Renal hemangioblastoma is rare.
Renal hemangioblastoma can mimic renal cell carcinoma on imaging, especially when hypervascular.
The lack of prominent feeding vessels does not exclude renal hemangioblastoma.
Small lesions may show inhomogeneous enhancement.
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is a major consideration.
A small enhancing cortical renal mass in a 60-year-old man is RCC until proven otherwise.
Clear cell RCC often shows arterial hyperenhancement.
Clear cell RCC can be subcapsular.
The lesion is extremely small, at 1 cm.
No other aggressive features are described for the lesion.
Papillary RCC is less likely.
Papillary RCC is typically hypovascular.
Papillary RCC enhances less avidly than the renal cortex.
The lesion showed obvious arterial-phase enhancement.
Fat-poor angiomyolipoma could present as a small enhancing renal mass without visible fat.
There is no mention of fat characteristics.
The enhancement pattern is less classic for fat-poor angiomyolipoma.
A metastatic lesion, including from thyroid, is considered.
Thyroid nodules are present.
Some metastases can be hypervascular.
TI-RADS 3 nodules are low suspicion.
There is no evidence of a primary thyroid malignancy.
The imaging describes a tiny renal subcapsular lesion with obvious arterial enhancement.
This pattern strongly overlaps with clear cell RCC.
This pattern is also classic for renal hemangioblastoma.
Renal hemangioblastoma is a rare benign tumor often mistaken for RCC.
The combination of a small round hypoechoic lesion, subcapsular location, and continuous obvious inhomogeneous arterial enhancement without prominent feeding vessels favors renal hemangioblastoma.
The most likely diagnosis is renal hemangioblastoma.
Renal hemangioblastoma is a high-probability differential diagnosis.
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is a high-probability differential diagnosis.
Papillary renal cell carcinoma is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
Fat-poor angiomyolipoma is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
Renal metastasis from thyroid or other primary is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
The final diagnosis is renal hemangioblastoma.
